outcome: No source I found settles the perfect komi for standard Go since 26 January 2024. The in-window items are on other boards or other games: a solve of the empty 5x5 board at komi 24.5 (arXiv preprint 9 May 2024, IJCAI 2024); an endgame-database study for boards up to 5x5 at komi 0 (Scientific Reports, 22 March 2024); a 7x7 Killall-Go solver with no komi (arXiv, 8 November 2024); and KataGo opening-book estimates for 9x9 optimal komi of 7 under area scoring and 6 under Japanese rules (updated 26 February 2026, and self-described as not a solution). The 19x19 estimates all predate the window.
problem_asks: One quantity: the komi at which perfect play by both sides makes a game of Go end in a draw (jigo), which the linked Wikipedia article glosses as the perfect value of komi. Unpacked: (a) the value itself, as a single number; (b) relative to a ruleset, since the statement names neither a board size nor a ruleset, so the usual reading is standard 19x19 Go, and the value may differ between area scoring (Tromp-Taylor, Chinese) and Japanese rules; (c) the value being exactly determined under perfect play, not merely estimated. No part asks about other board sizes. A result on another board or game does not answer it.

events.what_happened: Roger Clegg, 'The Value of the First Move', American Go Journal 12(3), 1977, cited by the Wikipedia Komi (Go) article (note 5) for its claim that under area scoring the perfect komi is an odd integer and that professional and computer statistics suggest 7. Bill Spight's forum post of 4 February 2019 reports that the 1977 article concluded the correct komi is 7 by Japanese rules, from Nihon Ki-in game statistics. I did not open the American Go Journal article; my account of it is second-hand.
events.delivers: A statistical estimate, from professional game results, that the komi balancing Japanese-rules games is 7. It argues from outcomes rather than perfect play, so it is not a game-theoretic value.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the value under perfect play, and the area-scoring value as a separate number.
events.doubts: Spight (lifein19x19 thread 'Komi in the AI age', 4 February 2019) says his own review of similar data put the 50:50 komi nearer 6.5. The Wikipedia odd-integer claim rests on this statistical argument, not on a game-theoretic result.
events.direction: Points to 7 under Japanese rules (and, via the Wikipedia gloss, to an odd integer under area scoring). It cuts toward a value, not toward a proof.

events.what_happened: Erik van der Werf and Mark Winands publish a solution of the 5x5 Go board in the ICGA Journal in 2003. The 2003 article was not opened. The year and venue come from the authors' 2009 paper as relayed in the Maastricht CRIS record I opened, which quotes the 2009 paper as saying 'In 2003, the Solution for the 5x5 Go board was published in this journal.' The ruleset and komi of the 2003 solve are not established from my sources.
events.delivers: A game-theoretic solution of the empty 5x5 board. Scope: one small board. The komi and ruleset were not established by me, and it gives no 19x19 value.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for 19x19 and other standard boards.
events.doubts: The same authors' 2009 paper says they identified errors in published human solutions. I did not establish whether the 5x5 result was among the human results they corrected. No independent re-check of the 2003 solve was found.
events.direction: A solved 5x5 board. It cuts toward no value for 19x19.
people: Erik C. D. van der Werf

events.what_happened: Erik van der Werf and Mark Winands, 'Solving Go for Rectangular Boards', ICGA Journal 32(2): 77-88, June 2009 (DOI 10.3233/ICG-2009-32203). Game-theoretic values for rectangular boards up to 30 intersections under Chinese rules, using an improved alpha-beta solver (MIGOS). The paper also compares published human solutions with the computer results and identifies errors in the human work. I read the publication record and an abstract paraphrase; the PDF was not readable through my fetch tool.
events.delivers: Game-theoretic values for rectangular boards up to 30 points under Chinese rules. A forum commenter says the largest solved board in it is 5x6. Scope: small rectangular boards only. 6x6 (36 points) and 7x7 (49 points) fall outside it, and it gives no 19x19 value.
events.remains: 6x6, 7x7, every board above 30 points including 19x19, and any Japanese-rules komi.
events.doubts: The values are stated under Chinese rules; the paper's abstract does not give a komi value. I did not read the value tables.
events.direction: Solved small rectangular boards. It cuts toward nothing on 19x19.
people: Erik C. D. van der Werf

events.what_happened: Francesco Morandin, Gianluca Amato, Rosa Gini, Carlo Metta, Maurizio Parton and Gian-Carlo Pascutto, 'SAI, a Sensible Artificial Intelligence that plays Go', arXiv 1809.03928 (v1 11 September 2018; later IJCNN 2019). According to the search summary of the full text, the paper says that the correct komi for 7x7 Go is known to be 9, with both players able to draw at that value, and that for 7x7 Leela Zero the authors chose 9.5 komi because they did not want to deal with draws. The arXiv abstract page I opened does not contain these sentences, so they are not verified against the paper. The 9 is cited as known, not derived.
events.revisions: A v2 exists (arXiv abs/1809.03928v2 appeared in search results). I did not compare versions.
events.delivers: Asserts that the 7x7 correct komi is 9. The sentence I saw in the search summary gives no derivation. Scope: 7x7 only.
events.remains: 19x19 and every other board. The Japanese-rules 7x7 value is also disputed by later KataGo analysis, which gives 8.
events.doubts: The 9 is stated without a source in the text I could see. KataGo analysis on lifein19x19 (April 2020) gives 8 under Japanese-like rules, so the 'known' claim is disputed for that ruleset.
events.direction: Asserts a 7x7 perfect komi of 9. It cuts toward that board only.

events.what_happened: Morandin, Amato, Fantozzi, Gini, Metta and Parton, 'SAI: a Sensible Artificial Intelligence that plays with handicap and targets high scores in 9x9 Go (extended version)', arXiv 1905.10863 (v1 26 May 2019). According to the search summary, the paper estimates the fair komi for 9x9 as 7, with two independent training runs agreeing. The arXiv abstract page I opened contains no komi sentence, so I could not confirm this from the paper.
events.delivers: If the search summary is accurate, a self-play estimate of 7 for 9x9. It is not a proof, and it is not verified against the paper.
events.doubts: A single program's self-play estimate. I could not confirm the sentence in the paper.
events.direction: A 9x9 estimate of 7. It cuts toward that board only.

events.what_happened: lightvector (David J. Wu, KataGo's developer), 'Perfect komi on 7x7 Go, Japanese rules', lifein19x19 thread p=256702, opening post 21 April 2020. KataGo's win rates from the 7x7 opening agree with 9 komi under Tromp-Taylor-like and Chinese-like rules (95% Black at 8.5, 5% at 9.5), and give 8 under Japanese-like rules (94% Black at 7.5, 11% Black at 8.5). The 9 for Japanese rules is attributed to a Sensei's Library 7x7 article by J. Davies, which the post says is contradicted by KataGo. Follow-ups: lightvector, 23 April 2020, says 'not even 6x6 has been fully exhaustively proven'; lightvector, 19 May 2020, says a 'fully rigorous solution is probably out of the question' and gives B+9 (Chinese) and B+8 (Japanese) as the best understanding. The KataGo 7x7 opening books (last updated 6 August 2021) list Tromp-Taylor komi 9 and Japanese-like komi 8, and state the Japanese-rules result was found earlier in 2020 with KataGo's help.
events.revisions: KataGo 7x7 books last updated 6 August 2021, giving Tromp-Taylor 9 and Japanese-like 8. The site states 'Optimal Komi in Japanese Rules is Probably 8, Not 9!'
events.delivers: KataGo self-play estimates for 7x7: komi 9 under area-scoring rules and 8 under Japanese-like rules. The author says a rigorous solution is out of reach. Scope: 7x7 only.
events.doubts: The author's own caveat: 'Of course there's always a chance KataGo missing something here too.' Forum replies disputed the Japanese value and the 'solved' status of 7x7 (see disputes). The Uberdude reply (23 April 2020) recalls that Li Zhe 6p 'claimed to have solved 7x7', and says 'It wasn't through an exhaustive search'. That is recollection, not verification.
events.direction: KataGo gives 9 under area-scoring rules and 8 under Japanese-like rules on 7x7. This cuts against the 9 that the forum post says is claimed for Japanese rules. It does not touch 19x19.

systems.name: KataGo
systems.what_it_did: Produced win-rate estimates from the 7x7 opening, from which the komi values 9 (area scoring) and 8 (Japanese-like rules) were read.

events.what_happened: Antti, 'Is fair komi necessarily an integer?', Nordic Go Dojo, 20 July 2020 (last edited 21 July 2020). Gives an artificial Japanese-rules (1989) position in which, at komi 6, Black's simplest line ends in an 11-11 draw; at komi 7 the same line is a one-point loss for Black; and at komi 6.5 neither side can win without a triple-ko 'no result', so 6.5 looks like the fair komi there. Concludes that it is not 'certain' the correct Japanese-rules komi is 6 or 7 points. The post also says recent evidence 'especially from the ai' points to 7 (Chinese rules) and 6 or 7 (Japanese rules). No AI system is named.
events.delivers: A constructed counterexample to the assumption that fair komi must be an integer, under Japanese rules. It is not a 19x19 result, and it gives no general perfect-komi value.
events.remains: The 19x19 Japanese-rules value, and whether the perfect komi of a full game must be a whole number.
events.directly_checkable: The Dia. 1 position can be checked by hand in principle under Japanese rules. I did not check it.
events.doubts: The position is artificial, and the author says so. From search summaries of a lifein19x19 thread on the post (not opened), a commenter says the ko and repetition options make the choice complicated, and another calls it a rules design mistake.
events.direction: Cuts against the integer premise in the Wikipedia odd-integer claim. It gives no value for 19x19.
events.object: A Japanese-rules (1989) position, Dia. 1, showing a fair komi of 6.5 under Japanese rules, so that fair komi need not be a whole number. The position is artificial and illustrates only that a counterexample exists. It is an explicit position, found by hand, not a non-constructive proof.

events.what_happened: lightvector (David J. Wu), 'AI opinions on fairest komi by board size', lifein19x19 thread p=259369 (opening post and fairest-komi table posted 27 August 2020). KataGo's self-play win rates from the opening position, using the final g170 40-block net, with 100k playouts on smaller boards and 10k on large boards, give for 19x19: Japanese rules fairest komi 6.5, with 'Unclear if perfect komi is 6 or 7, enough that fairest komi in practice is 6.5'; Chinese rules fairest komi 7, 'Pretty much fair in practice'. Follow-ups: gennan (28 August 2020) reads 6 as perfect komi for Japanese rules and 7 for Chinese rules. Uberdude (4 November 2020) reports that KataGo now prefers White on Japanese 6.5. lightvector (5 November 2020) answers 'Not sure' and points to the published nets. Elom0 (14 August 2023) says only 'An update of this data on' and gives no update.
events.revisions: No update found. Elom0 (14 August 2023) promises an update of the data, with no follow-up that I could find.
events.delivers: A KataGo self-play estimate for 19x19: fairest komi 6.5 under Japanese rules, with perfect komi 'unclear' between 6 and 7; fairest komi 7 under Chinese rules. Scope: 19x19 under the two rulesets, with an estimated value, not a proof.
events.remains: The perfect komi under perfect play for both rulesets: the 6-or-7 question under Japanese rules, and any exact Chinese-rules value.

checked_by.qualification: Lifein19x19 forum participants; qualifications not established
checked_by.what_they_did: Commented on the table and read off values (gennan: 6 for Japanese, 7 for Chinese). These are replies, not verifications.

events.doubts: A single 2020 network (g170, 40 blocks), at 100k playouts on small boards and 10k on large ones. The author says these results 'might differ from the actual rules in pathological positions'. The Japanese-rules 19x19 value is explicitly unresolved ('6 or 7'). The Nordic Go Dojo counterexample (2020) argues the perfect komi need not be a whole number. No 2025 or 2026 19x19 KataGo analysis was found.
events.direction: Japanese rules: fairest komi 6.5, with perfect komi 6 or 7. Chinese rules: fairest komi 7, pretty much fair in practice. The estimate points to 6 to 7 and gives no proof.

systems.name: KataGo
systems.what_it_did: Produced the self-play win rates from which the 19x19 'fairest komi' and perfect-komi estimates were read.
systems.basis_quote: I did a study of KataGo's opinions about the "fairest" komi for each square board size using the final 40 block network.

ai.disclosed_cost: Playouts stated per board size: 100k on smaller boards, 10k on large boards.

events.what_happened: Li Zhe (6p, Wuhan University), keynote 'Knowledge of Go in the AI Age' at the European Go Congress (EGC) 2023. The announcement page I opened is dated 3 August 2023 and says the talk was on 'calculating the optimal solution for small boards and the structure of go thinking'. The slide PDF (uploaded August 2023) was too large for my fetch tool. Per search summaries of the slides only (unverified): balanced komi for 6x6 is 2 stones or 3 territory, with optimal solutions 'not unique'; 7x7 balanced komi is 9 under Tromp-Taylor and 8 under Japanese rules, the Japanese value credited to a 2021 KataGo analysis; the optimality of 7x7 and 8x8 is 'not yet possible to prove'; 9x9 is beyond human and current AI calculation. The talk date is inferred as 1 August 2023 from the congress schedule, not stated.
events.delivers: Per the slide summaries only (unverified): balanced-komi values for 6x6 and 7x7 on the board sizes it covers. Scope: small boards only.
events.remains: 19x19, a rigorous proof of optimality for 7x7 or 8x8, and any 19x19 value.
events.doubts: A lifein19x19 forum recollection (Uberdude, April 2020, before this talk) says Li Zhe 6p 'claimed to have solved 7x7', and that it was not through exhaustive search. The 2023 slides themselves are said to state that optimality cannot yet be proven. The slide content is unverified because I could not read the PDF.
events.direction: Per the slide summaries: 7x7 balanced komi 9 (Tromp-Taylor) and 8 (Japanese). This agrees with KataGo's 2020 and 2021 values, and does not reach 19x19.

events.what_happened: KataGo Opening Books (katagobooks.org, copyright David J Wu). The 9x9 books were first posted in October 2023 (per the site's update history). The main page states: 'For each ruleset, we use the komi believed to be optimal for that size', and lists the 9x9 Tromp-Taylor book at komi 7 and the Japanese-like book at komi 6, both last updated 26 February 2026. The site says 'Optimal komi for 9x9 appears to be 7 in area-scoring rules and 6 in Japanese scoring rules.' The 9x9 highlights page says that under both rulesets there are four distinct optimal first moves, and that all of them give Black a lead of 7 points before komi under area scoring and 6 under Japanese rules. The 26 February 2026 update expanded the 9x9 books by about 70% and changed the evaluation of various lines 'from drawing to winning/losing, or vice versa'.
events.revisions: Oct 2023: 9x9 books first posted. Nov 2024: more 9x9 variations added. 26 Feb 2026: 9x9 books expanded about 70%; komi and line evaluations changed. I did not verify whether the 2023 pages already stated the komi values. The date above is the books' origin, not a verified date for the komi wording.
events.delivers: A bot estimate that the optimal komi on 9x9 is 7 under area scoring and 6 under Japanese scoring. The site explicitly does not claim a rigorous solution. Scope: 9x9 only.
events.remains: 19x19, any rigorous 9x9 result, and a proof that either komi value is optimal.
events.time_since_posted: about 3 years, for the books' origin; the komi values as currently stated date from February 2026
events.doubts: The site's own caveats: 'There are almost certainly some deep misevaluations and mistakes in the 9x9 books.' It also says KataGo's books for 9x9 'are very far from being comprehensive' and that 'Unlike in small opening books where we can achieve very high confidence that a deviation is objectively wrong, for 9x9, KataGo is not confident.' The February 2026 update changed several lines between draw and win or loss, so the estimate has moved within the last year. Scores in the books are described as approximate.
events.direction: Area scoring: optimal komi 7 on 9x9. Japanese rules: optimal komi 6 on 9x9. The site's own sentence says that under both rulesets Black is ahead by 7 (area) or 6 (Japanese) before komi. It cuts toward a 9x9 value, not 19x19.

systems.name: KataGo
systems.what_it_did: Generated the opening books, including the komi values for 9x9 under each ruleset. The site describes the 9x9, 8x8 and 7x7 books as coming from KataGo's main effort.
systems.basis_quote: For each ruleset, we use the komi believed to be optimal for that size.

events.what_happened: Chia-Ming Hsu, Hung-Cheng Lin, Yueh-Ting Chen, Chih-Wen Hsueh and Tsan-sheng Hsu, 'Construction, observation and knowledge abstraction for go endgames on small boards', Scientific Reports 14:6903 (received 31 May 2023, accepted 18 March 2024, published 22 March 2024; DOI 10.1038/s41598-024-57338-x). They build endgame databases of optimal values and moves for every legal arrangement on N x N boards with 1 < N <= 5, with komi set to 0 ('Finally, we set the komi to 0'). They also use KataGo as a difficulty measure: 4x4 puzzles are input to KataGo and the time it takes to solve them is recorded. The paper reports that the optimal values differ by board parity, and that even boards are balanced when cycles are allowed. An earlier NTU thesis by the same group (2022 per a search summary, unverified) covered the 4x4 case.
events.revisions: Received 31 May 2023, accepted 18 March 2024, published 22 March 2024. The earlier NTU thesis may be the first public written version. I did not open it and did not verify its date. If that thesis is the first public version, the event moves earlier.
events.delivers: Optimal values and moves for endgame positions (all legal arrangements) on square boards with 1 < N <= 5, at komi 0. This covers endgame positions on small boards, not full-board game values, and it sets no komi.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the full-board perfect komi, on 19x19 and on any other board.
events.doubts: The paper uses komi 0 throughout, so its values do not transfer to the komi question. The authors note possible shortcomings of KataGo's difficulty measure.
events.direction: Endgame values on boards up to 5x5 at komi 0. It bears on small-board endgames and not on a full-board perfect komi.

systems.name: KataGo
systems.what_it_did: Used as a difficulty measure: 4x4 puzzles were input to KataGo and the solve time was recorded as an indicator of difficulty. KataGo did not compute the endgame database values.
systems.basis_quote: Therefore, the time taken by KataGo can be used as a measure of the difficulty of a problem.

events.what_happened: Owen Randall, Martin Muller, Ting-Han Wei and Ryan Hayward (University of Alberta), 'Expected Work Search: Combining Win Rate and Proof Size Estimation', arXiv 2405.05594 (v1 submitted 9 May 2024), IJCAI 2024 main track, pp. 7003-7011. The paper states: 'For Go, we present the first solution to the empty 5x5 board with the commonly used positional superko ruleset.' Table 2 gives the 5x5 komi as 24.5, with EWS solving it in 5.252 hours using 6 parallel processes (2,605,781,360 nodes). Section 5.2.1 says the 5x5 board was solved 'with the positional superko ruleset, confirming the full-board first player win for Japanese rules'.
events.revisions: v1 9 May 2024 (arXiv). Published at IJCAI 2024, pp. 7003-7011 (August 2024). I did not check later arXiv versions.
events.delivers: The empty 5x5 board under positional superko, at komi 24.5, is a first-player full-board win (the paper's words). Scope: one 5x5 board, one ruleset, one komi value. The paper gives no score margin and no perfect-komi value.
events.remains: The 19x19 perfect komi; every other board size; the komi at which 5x5 is balanced under perfect play, which a single solve at komi 24.5 does not determine.

checked_by.qualification: Peer review at a refereed AI conference; reviewers are not named in the proceedings
checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication. This is a refereed acceptance, not a public verification of the solve.

events.directly_checkable: The 5x5 solve is reproducible in principle with a Go solver. I did not reproduce it, and I found no third-party reproduction.
events.doubts: The paper's own wording is inconsistent: the introduction says positional superko, while Section 5.2.1 says 'for Japanese rules'. The paper does not say what the perfect komi on 5x5 is, and a solve at komi 24.5 fixes only one komi value. A web search for later citations found none. I did not check Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar directly.
events.direction: A solved outcome on a 5x5 board, at komi 24.5, with a first-player full-board win. It does not cut for or against the 19x19 komi question.

events.what_happened: Yun-Jui Tsai, Ting Han Wei, Chi-Huang Lin, Chung-Chin Shih, Hung Guei, I-Chen Wu and Ti-Rong Wu, 'Solving 7x7 Killall-Go with Seki Database', arXiv 2411.05565 (submitted 8 November 2024). The paper enumerates seki patterns up to a set area and stores them in a table that the solver uses to recognise mutual life. The abstract reports that a day-long unsolvable position was solved in 482 seconds with the table. The game is Killall-Go, not standard Go. The abstract does not mention komi or scoring rules.
events.revisions: v1 8 November 2024. I did not check later versions.
events.delivers: A search technique for solving 7x7 Killall-Go. It is a different game with no komi, so it establishes nothing about the perfect komi of standard Go.
events.doubts: Not relevant to komi. The abstract is the only part I read.
events.direction: Solves a 7x7 Killall-Go technique, which does not touch the komi question.

disputes.summary: 7x7 Japanese-rules komi: 9 vs 8. The 2018 SAI paper (as cited in search summaries) and a Sensei's Library 7x7 article by J. Davies, relayed in the April 2020 forum thread, give 9 for Japanese rules. KataGo analysis (April 2020), the KataGo 7x7 books (last updated August 2021) and the Li Zhe 2023 slides (as summarised) give 8. The KataGo site says the 8 was discovered earlier in 2020 with KataGo's help.

Whether 7x7 Go is solved. Forum recollection: Li Zhe 6p 'claimed to have solved 7x7' (2015 or earlier, not exhaustive). Unsourced forum claim (April 2020) that 7x7 'has been solved already by brute force'. Lightvector and Uberdude reply that no exhaustive proof exists. The KataGo 7x7 books state they 'do NOT solve 7x7 Go' in the rigorous sense. A 2023 blog post states flatly that Go is solved on 7x7 (search summary only, not opened). The 2023 Li Zhe slides say optimality cannot yet be proven (search summary).

Whether the perfect komi must be a whole number. The Wikipedia article states that under area scoring without seki the perfect komi is an odd integer (citing Clegg 1977). The Nordic Go Dojo post (July 2020) gives an artificial Japanese-rules counterexample in which fair komi is 6.5, so the integer premise is not established.

19x19 Japanese-rules perfect komi: 6 or 7 (lightvector's 2020 table says unclear, with 6.5 as the practical fairest komi); gennan reads 6; Uberdude (November 2020) reports KataGo now prefers White at Japanese 6.5; Clegg 1977 (as relayed) gives 7; Spight's 2019 reanalysis gives 6.5. These are estimates from different methods and do not conflict as proofs, but they disagree on the value.

The EWS paper (arXiv 2405.05594) says the 5x5 solve is under positional superko in its introduction and abstract, but Section 5.2.1 describes the full-board first-player win as 'for Japanese rules'. The solve's ruleset is therefore ambiguous within the source.

summary: Thirty-seven web searches (listed below) and about thirty page fetches (several failed or returned unreadable binary). No source I found reports a perfect komi for standard 19x19 Go, and none claims one was determined since 26 January 2024. The Wikipedia Komi (Go) article, as last edited 18 September 2026 per the fetched page, still says the perfect komi 'is not known with certainty'. Its 'odd integer, 7 points' claim is attributed to a 1977 statistical article (Clegg). The 19x19 evidence is all pre-window and all estimated, not solved: lightvector's 2020 KataGo self-play table (fairest komi 6.5 under Japanese rules with perfect komi 'unclear' between 6 and 7; 7 under Chinese rules, 'pretty much fair in practice'); the 2020 Nordic Go Dojo counterexample, which argues fair komi need not be an integer; and the 1977 statistics. In-window events concern other boards or games: (i) EWS, arXiv 9 May 2024 (IJCAI 2024), solves the empty 5x5 board under positional superko at komi 24.5, reported as a first-player full-board win; the paper gives no score margin and no perfect-komi value, and it names no learned or language model (the algorithm combines MCTS-style win-rate estimation with proof-number-search proof-size estimation and is placed in cs.AI); (ii) Hsu et al., Scientific Reports, published 22 March 2024, computes endgame databases for 1 < N <= 5 at komi 0, with KataGo used only as a difficulty measure; (iii) Tsai et al., arXiv 8 November 2024, solves 7x7 Killall-Go, a different game with no komi; (iv) KataGo Opening Books, whose 9x9 entry gives optimal komi 7 under area scoring and 6 under Japanese rules, last updated 26 February 2026 and expanded by about 70%, with the site's own statements that 9x9 is 'very far from being comprehensive' and that the books are not a solution. The 7x7 entry says explicitly that the books 'do NOT solve 7x7 Go'. Close calls: (a) the 9x9 KataGo estimate is recorded as an event dated to the books' origin (October 2023), since I could not verify when the komi wording first appeared, so its place inside or outside the window depends on that date; (b) EWS is recorded with none_found true, since it is a classical search algorithm with no named model, but some would count MCTS-based search as AI, and the judging pass should decide; (c) the 5x5 solve at komi 24.5 is one komi value on one board, so by itself it does not locate the balanced komi on 5x5. AI search: I searched for LLM, GPT, Gemini, Claude and AlphaGo claims about komi and found none. The only AI-linked komi results are KataGo estimates and the EWS paper, which names no model. The lifein19x19 page headers that read 'It is currently ... 2025' are scrape dates, not post dates, and I did not date any event from them. Three PDFs (the Li Zhe slides, the 2009 ICGA paper and the EWS PDF) could not be read through my fetch tool, which returned raw binary, so the quotes from them come from HTML pages, abstracts, or search summaries and are not checked against the raw text.
competing_reading: The 2020 KataGo 19x19 table, the 9x9 books and the 5x5 solve could be read together as the game-theoretic komi programme making real progress, so that the problem has 'moved' in the window through the 5x5 solve and the Feb 2026 9x9 update, and should be classed as partially advanced rather than unchanged. Against that: the 5x5 solve is one komi value on one board under one ruleset, the 9x9 values are self-described estimates that the 2026 update changed, and the question is about standard 19x19 Go. A second reading: the KataGo 9x9 and 19x19 numbers are AI estimates of the perfect komi, and a judging pass that counts AI-produced estimates would record an AI contribution that the 'solved' reading would not. Against that: the books and forum tables are not claims of a result on the problem as stated.
what_would_settle_it: For standard Go, a rigorous game-theoretic value for 19x19 with its ruleset, which nothing in the sources approaches. For the in-window events: the full text of arXiv 2405.05594 for the 5x5 score margin and whether the komi-to-outcome relation is given; later citations of EWS that extend it to 6x6 or 7x7, checked on Google Scholar or Semantic Scholar, which I did not do; the first archived version of the KataGo 9x9 komi statement, to date the komi wording and not just the books; the date of the NTU thesis behind Hsu et al.; and the text of the Li Zhe slide deck and the 2009 ICGA value tables.

judgement.why: The statement asks for the perfect komi of Go, which in its usual reading means the standard 19x19 game. Every small-board result (5x5, rectangular boards up to 30 points, 7x7, 9x9, endgame databases at komi 0) and the Killall-Go solver answer a changed question, so they are variant. Some of them are rigorous solves of their own boards, but that does not make them a case of the 19x19 question. The 19x19 evidence is all statistical or self-play estimation from before the snapshot (Clegg 1977, the KataGo 2020 table). An estimate neither determines the value nor proves a bound on it, so these are none. The Nordic counterexample shows only that fair komi need not be an integer in an artificial position; it settles nothing about the value, so it is none and its object does not bear on the statement. The KataGo rows are generated, since the estimates themselves are KataGo output, but all of them are discarded on scope. EWS is a classical search algorithm with no learned model named, so its role is none. The 9x9 books cannot be placed after the snapshot from the record: they originate in October 2023, and the date the komi wording first appeared is unverified. Being variant, this does not matter for the outcome.
judgement.doubts: One could argue that small-board perfect komi is a 'case' of a statement that names no board size. I read the statement as standard Go, the reading the record also gives. Either way, no after-snapshot event determines a perfect komi on any board: EWS solves 5x5 at a single komi only.
